lessons.title: Protein Metabolism: Transamination, Deamination, Ammonia Toxicity, Urea Cycle*** & Glycine

slides.h: 1. Transamination, Deamination, Ammonia Fate & Ammonia Toxicity
slides.p: Dietary/intracellular proteins are hydrolyzed to amino acids; amino nitrogen enters central metabolism via transamination and deamination:
bullets: Transamination (Aminotransferases / Transaminases — PLP / Vitamin B₆ coenzyme): Transfers α-amino group from an amino acid to α-ketoglutarate → glutamate (and oxaloacetate ↔ aspartate, pyruvate ↔ alanine). (Lysine, threonine, proline, hydroxyproline do NOT undergo transamination).

Deamination & Ammonia Fate: Oxidative deamination by hepatic/renal glutamate dehydrogenase (NAD⁺/NADP⁺) releases free NH₃/NH₄⁺; non-oxidative deamination acts on serine/threonine (PLP). Ammonia is trapped safely as non-toxic glutamine (glutamine synthetase) and alanine (glucose-alanine cycle) for transport to liver/kidney.

Ammonia Toxicity (Hepatic Encephalopathy): High blood NH₃/NH₄⁺ depletes α-ketoglutarate (forming glutamate/glutamine), slowing the TCA cycle and ATP synthesis in brain, altering neurotransmitters (glutamate/GABA), and causing cerebral edema, asterixis (flapping tremor), confusion, and coma.
slides.remember: Transaminases need Vitamin B₆ (PLP)! High NH₃ depletes α-ketoglutarate → slows brain TCA cycle & ATP → Hepatic encephalopathy!
slides.q: Which vitamin-derived coenzyme is required by aminotransferase (transaminase) enzymes?
slides.why: Aminotransferases use pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), the active coenzyme form of vitamin B₆, to shuttle amino groups between amino acids and keto acids.

slides.h: 2. Urea Cycle*** (5 Steps, Energetics & Defects) + Glycine Specialized Products
slides.p: The urea cycle*** (Krebs-Henseleit / ornithine cycle) detoxifies ammonia into water-soluble urea in periportal hepatocytes (partially mitochondrial, mostly cytosolic):
bullets: 5 Steps & Rate-Limiting Enzyme: 1. NH₃ + CO₂ + 2 ATP → Carbamoyl phosphate via mitochondrial Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS-I) (rate-limiting; allosterically activated by N-acetylglutamate [NAG]!). 2. Carbamoyl phosphate + Ornithine → Citrulline (ornithine transcarbamoylase; transported to cytosol). 3. Citrulline + Aspartate + ATP (→ AMP + PPi, equiv. to 2 ATP) → Argininosuccinate (argininosuccinate synthetase). 4. Cleaved to Arginine + Fumarate (argininosuccinase; fumarate links to TCA cycle!). 5. Arginine → Urea + Ornithine (arginase; 4 high-energy phosphate bonds consumed per urea molecule).

Urea Cycle Disorders & Glycine: Enzyme defects (e.g., OTC deficiency) cause hyperammonemia, vomiting, encephalopathy. Glycine (simplest amino acid; synthesized from serine/glyoxylate; inhibited by benzoate via hippurate) forms heme, purines, creatine, glutathione, bile salts (glycocholate), and collagen.
slides.remember: CPS-I is rate-limiting & needs N-acetylglutamate (NAG)! Urea cycle costs 4 ATP equivalents! Glycine makes Heme, Purines, Creatine & Glutathione!
slides.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting first step of the urea cycle in liver mitochondria and requires N-acetylglutamate as an allosteric activator?
slides.why: Mitochondrial CPS-I catalyzes carbamoyl phosphate synthesis—the committed/rate-limiting step of the urea cycle—and is allosterically activated by N-acetylglutamate.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Transamination & deamination → Ammonia transport & toxicity mechanism → Urea cycle*** (5 steps, CPS-I + NAG, 4 ATP equivalents, fumarate link, hyperammonemia) + diagram → Glycine synthesis & specialized products.

lessons.title: Tyrosine & Phenylalanine Metabolism, Inborn Errors*, Alkaptonuria & Biogenic Amines

slides.h: 1. Phenylalanine → Tyrosine Pathway & Phenylketonuria (PKU) / Alkaptonuria
slides.p: Essential phenylalanine is hydroxylated to tyrosine by phenylalanine hydroxylase (requires tetrahydrobiopterin [BH₄] cofactor):
bullets: Phenylketonuria (PKU — Phenylalanine hydroxylase or BH₄ defect): Phenylalanine accumulates and forms phenylpyruvate/phenyllactate/phenylacetate; causes severe intellectual disability, hypopigmentation (low melanin), musty/mousy odor; treated with low-phenylalanine diet.

Alkaptonuria (Homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency — Vitamin C cofactor): Autosomal recessive block in tyrosine catabolism → homogentisic acid accumulates and is excreted in urine, turning dark/black on standing or alkalinization; late ochronosis (bluish-black pigment in cartilage/connective tissue) and ochronotic arthritis.
slides.remember: PKU = Phenylalanine hydroxylase defect (needs BH₄). Alkaptonuria = Homogentisate oxidase defect → Urine turns BLACK on standing + Ochronosis!
slides.q: Alkaptonuria is caused by a genetic deficiency of which enzyme in the tyrosine catabolic pathway?
slides.why: Deficiency of homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase leads to accumulation and urinary excretion of homogentisic acid, which oxidizes to a dark pigment on standing.

slides.h: 2. Specialized Products of Tyrosine & Biogenic Amines
slides.p: Tyrosine is the precursor for vital hormones, pigments, and neurotransmitters, while amino acid decarboxylation yields biogenic amines:
bullets: Tyrosine Derivatives: Melanin (via DOPA by tyrosinase — absent in albinism), Catecholamines (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine), and Thyroid hormones (T₃, T₄).

Biogenic Amines (Decarboxylation via PLP / Vitamin B₆): Histidine → Histamine (gastric acid, allergic vasodilation/bronchoconstriction); Tyrosine → Tyramine / Catecholamines; Tryptophan → Serotonin (5-HT) & Melatonin; Glutamate → GABA (inhibitory neurotransmitter).
slides.remember: Tyrosinase makes Melanin (absent in Albinism)! Amino acid decarboxylases need PLP (Vit B₆) to make Biogenic Amines (Histamine, Serotonin, GABA)!
slides.q: Which enzyme deficiency results in oculocutaneous albinism due to impaired melanin synthesis from tyrosine?
slides.why: Tyrosinase catalyzes the conversion of tyrosine to DOPA and dopaquinone in melanocytes; its deficiency causes albinism.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Phenylalanine → Tyrosine pathway → PKU & Alkaptonuria (biochemical basis, urine darkening, ochronosis, Benedict's/ferric chloride tests) → Tyrosine products (melanin, catecholamines, T₃/T₄) → Biogenic amines.

lessons.title: Nucleotide Metabolism: Purine Salvage Pathway**, Purine Catabolism, Hyperuricemia & Gout**

slides.h: 1. Purine Salvage Pathway** (APRT & HGPRT / Lesch-Nyhan)
slides.p: Because de novo purine synthesis is energy-expensive (6 ATP equivalents), cells recycle free purine bases via the purine salvage pathway** using PRPP (5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate):
bullets: Two Key Salvage Enzymes: 1. Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase (APRT): Adenine + PRPP → AMP + PPi. 2. Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT): Hypoxanthine + PRPP → IMP + PPi; Guanine + PRPP → GMP + PPi.

Lesch-Nyhan Syndrome (X-linked recessive HGPRT deficiency): Severe hyperuricemia & gout, neurological dysfunction, intellectual disability, and characteristic compulsive self-mutilation (lip/finger biting); elevated PRPP accelerates de novo purine synthesis.
slides.remember: HGPRT salvages Hypoxanthine & Guanine using PRPP! HGPRT deficiency = Lesch-Nyhan syndrome (hyperuricemia + self-mutilation)!
slides.q: Deficiency of which purine salvage enzyme causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome?
slides.why: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked disorder caused by deficiency of HGPRT, leading to hyperuricemia, gout, and neurobehavioral abnormalities.

slides.h: 2. Purine Catabolism to Uric Acid, Hyperuricemia & Gout**
slides.p: In humans (who lack uricase), purine nucleosides/nucleotides are catabolized to uric acid (end product excreted in urine):
bullets: Catabolic Steps: AMP → IMP/adenosine → inosine → hypoxanthine; GMP → guanosine → guanine → xanthine. Xanthine oxidase (molybdenum/iron enzyme) converts hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid.

Hyperuricemia & Gout**: Elevated serum uric acid (>7 mg/dL in men, >6 mg/dL in women) leads to monosodium urate crystal deposition in joints (gouty arthritis, classically first metatarsophalangeal joint / podagra), tophi, and uric acid renal stones. Treated with Allopurinol (competitive inhibitor of xanthine oxidase), febuxostat, uricosurics, or colchicine.
slides.remember: Xanthine oxidase makes Uric acid! Allopurinol inhibits Xanthine oxidase to treat Gout!
slides.q: How does allopurinol lower uric acid levels in patients with chronic gout?
opts: By activating carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I
slides.why: Allopurinol (and its active metabolite oxypurinol) inhibits xanthine oxidase, blocking the conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid.

lessons.exam: SN order: Purine salvage pathway** (PRPP, APRT & HGPRT, Lesch-Nyhan syndrome) → Purine catabolism to uric acid via xanthine oxidase → Hyperuricemia & Gout** (urate crystals, tophi, allopurinol action).

lessons.title: Heme Biosynthesis & Regulation*, Porphyria, Heme Catabolism, Bilirubin/Jaundice & Hemoglobinopathies**

slides.h: 1. Heme Biosynthesis, ALA Synthase Regulation*, Porphyrias & Hb Variants**
slides.p: Heme is synthesized from Glycine + Succinyl-CoA (8 steps, starting and ending in mitochondria); δ-Aminolevulinic acid (ALA) synthase-1 (ALAS1) is the rate-limiting enzyme (requires PLP / Vitamin B₆; repressed by heme via feedback inhibition and induced by drugs/cytochrome P450):
bullets: Porphyrias: Enzyme defects in heme synthesis cause accumulation of porphyrins/precursors (e.g., Acute Intermittent Porphyria — porphobilinogen deaminase defect: abdominal pain, neuropsychiatric symptoms, port-wine urine, NO photosensitivity).

Hemoglobinopathies** (Single Amino Acid Substitutions in β-globin): Sickle-cell hemoglobin (HbS): Glutamate → Valine at position 6 of β-chain (hydrophobic patch causes sickling under low O₂); HbC: Glutamate → Lysine at position 6 of β-chain.
slides.remember: ALA synthase (needs Vit B₆) is rate-limiting in Heme synthesis! HbS = Glu6 → Val6 on β-chain!
slides.q: Which amino acid substitution in the β-globin chain gives rise to sickle-cell hemoglobin (HbS)?
opts: Valine replaced by Glutamate at position 6
Glutamate replaced by Valine at position 6
Glutamate replaced by Lysine at position 6
Histidine replaced by Tyrosine at position 8
slides.why: In HbS, a point mutation replaces hydrophilic glutamate at position 6 of the β-globin chain with hydrophobic valine.

slides.h: 2. Heme Catabolism, Bilirubin Fate & Classification of Jaundice
slides.p: Senescent RBCs (~120 days) are destroyed in reticuloendothelial macrophages: Heme → Biliverdin (heme oxygenase, releases CO & Fe³⁺) → Unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin (biliverdin reductase), bound to albumin in blood:
bullets: Hepatic Conjugation & Gut Fate: Hepatocytes take up unconjugated bilirubin (ligandin/Y-protein) and conjugate it with glucuronic acid via UDP-glucuronyl transferase → water-soluble conjugated (direct) bilirubin secreted in bile → converted by gut bacteria to stercobilinogen/stercobilin (fecal color) and urobilinogen (reabsorbed/urinary).

Three Types of Jaundice: 1. Hemolytic (pre-hepatic): ↑Unconjugated bilirubin, ↑urine urobilinogen, normal stools, NO bilirubin in urine (unconjugated is water-insoluble/albumin-bound). 2. Hepatocellular (hepatic): Mixed ↑conjugated & unconjugated bilirubin, ↑transaminases (ALT/AST). 3. Obstructive (post-hepatic / cholestatic): ↑Conjugated bilirubin in blood & urine, pale clay-colored stools, absent/low urobilinogen, ↑alkaline phosphatase.
slides.remember: UDP-glucuronyl transferase makes Conjugated (direct) bilirubin! Hemolytic = ↑Unconjugated; Obstructive = ↑Conjugated + Clay stools + Bilirubin in urine!
slides.q: Which enzyme conjugates bilirubin with glucuronic acid in hepatocytes to form water-soluble conjugated (direct) bilirubin?
slides.why: Hepatic UDP-glucuronyl transferase transfers glucuronate to unconjugated bilirubin, converting it into water-soluble conjugated bilirubin.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Heme biosynthesis & ALAS regulation* → Intermittent porphyria → HbS & HbC amino acid changes** → Heme degradation to bilirubin & enterohepatic fate → Hemolytic, hepatocellular & obstructive jaundice comparison.

lessons.title: Vitamins: Vitamin A** (Wald's Cycle), Vitamin D (Hormone), Thiamine*, B₆, B₉/B₁₂ & Vitamin C

slides.h: 1. Vitamin A** (Wald's Visual Cycle & Deficiency) & Vitamin D (Calciferol Hormone)
slides.p: Master these two fat-soluble vitamins for both LAQs and Short Notes:
bullets: Vitamin A** (Retinol/Retinal/Retinoic Acid): Deficiency causes night blindness (nyctalopia), xerophthalmia, Bitot's spots, keratomalacia, follicular hyperkeratosis, impaired immunity. In Wald's visual cycle, light isomerizes 11-cis retinal → all-trans retinal, separating from opsin (bleaching rhodopsin); all-trans retinol returns to pigment epithelium to regenerate 11-cis retinal.

Vitamin D (Cholecalciferol D₃ / Ergocalciferol D₂ — Pre-hormone/Hormone): Activated via 25-hydroxylation in liver (25-(OH)D / calcidiol) and 1α-hydroxylation in kidney proximal tubule (PTH-stimulated → 1,25-(OH)₂D₃ / calcitriol, active steroid-like hormone raising serum Ca²⁺ & PO₄³⁻). Deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.
slides.remember: Wald's cycle = 11-cis retinal → light → all-trans retinal! Calcitriol = 1,25-(OH)₂D₃ (activated in Liver [25] & Kidney [1α])!
slides.q: Which two organs sequentially hydroxylate vitamin D₃ (cholecalciferol) to produce active 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol)?
slides.why: Cholecalciferol is converted to 25-hydroxycholecalciferol in the liver and then to active 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol) in the kidney.

slides.h: 2. Thiamine* (B₁), Pyridoxine (B₆), Folate (B₉), Cobalamin (B₁₂) & Vitamin C
slides.p: Complete your Vitamins review with coenzyme roles and deficiency syndromes:
bullets: Thiamine* (B₁ → TPP coenzyme): Required for oxidative decarboxylation (pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase) & transketolase (HMP shunt). Deficiency causes beriberi (dry/neuropathic, wet/cardiac) and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.
Pyridoxine (B₆ → PLP coenzyme): Transaminases, decarboxylases (biogenic amines/GABA), δ-ALA synthase (heme), glycogen phosphorylase.

Folic Acid (THF) & Vitamin B₁₂ (Methylcobalamin / Adenosylcobalamin): Both are essential for one-carbon metabolism and DNA synthesis (thymidylate synthesis); deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia (B₁₂ deficiency also causes subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord due to methylmalonyl-CoA mutase/methionine synthase dysfunction; requires intrinsic factor for absorption).

Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid): Cofactor for prolyl & lysyl hydroxylases (collagen cross-linking/maturation), iron absorption, antioxidant; deficiency causes scurvy (bleeding gums, poor wound healing, petechiae/hemorrhages).
slides.remember: B₁ (TPP) = Beriberi & Wernicke-Korsakoff! B₉ & B₁₂ = Megaloblastic anemia (B₁₂ also causes neurological degeneration)! Vit C = Collagen hydroxylation & Scurvy!
slides.q: Deficiency of which vitamin causes megaloblastic anemia accompanied by neurological degeneration (subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord)?
slides.why: Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency impairs both DNA synthesis (causing megaloblastic anemia) and myelin/methylmalonyl-CoA metabolism (causing neuropathic/spinal cord lesions).

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Vitamin A** (Wald's visual cycle & deficiency) → Vitamin D (25 & 1α activation as hormone, rickets/osteomalacia) → Thiamine* (TPP & beriberi) → B₆ (PLP), Folate & B₁₂ (megaloblastic anemia) → Vitamin C (collagen & scurvy).

lessons.title: Enzymes: Kinetics, Km & E-S Complex, Competitive/Non-Competitive Inhibition & Isoenzymes*** (MI)

slides.h: 1. Enzyme Activity Factors, Activation Energy, E-S Complex & Km Value
slides.p: Enzymes are protein biocatalysts (except ribozymes) that lower activation energy by stabilizing the transition state via an Enzyme–Substrate (ES) complex without altering reaction ΔG° or equilibrium:
bullets: Factors Affecting Velocity (V): Enzyme concentration (linear proportionality at excess substrate), substrate concentration ([S] — hyperbolic Michaelis-Menten curve approaching V_max), temperature (optimum ~37°C; denaturation above ~45–50°C), and pH (optimum pH & ionization of active-site groups).

Michaelis Constant (K_m): Substrate concentration at which reaction velocity reaches half of maximum velocity (1/2 V_max); inversely measures enzyme–substrate affinity (low K_m = high affinity; glucokinase has high K_m for glucose vs hexokinase's low K_m).
slides.remember: Enzymes lower Activation Energy! K_m = [S] at 1/2 V_max (Lower K_m = Higher affinity)!
slides.q: What does the Michaelis constant (K_m) of an enzyme represent?
opts: The substrate concentration required to achieve half-maximal velocity (1/2 V_max)
The turnover number (k_cat) multiplied by enzyme concentration
The free energy change (ΔG) of the reaction
slides.why: K_m is defined as the substrate concentration at which initial reaction velocity is half of V_max, serving as an inverse measure of substrate affinity.

slides.h: 2. Competitive vs Non-Competitive Inhibition & Isoenzymes*** (Myocardial Infarction**)
slides.p: Compare enzyme inhibitors and clinical diagnostic/therapeutic enzymes & isoenzymes:
bullets: Competitive vs Non-Competitive Inhibition: Competitive inhibitor structurally resembles substrate and binds the active site → increases apparent K_m (decreases affinity) but V_max is unchanged (overcome by high [S]; e.g., statins/HMG-CoA reductase, malonate/succinate dehydrogenase). Non-competitive inhibitor binds a different (allosteric/non-active) site regardless of substrate binding → V_max decreases (cannot be overcome by high [S]) while K_m is unchanged.

Isoenzymes*** & Myocardial Infarction**: Multiple molecular forms of an enzyme catalyzing the same reaction with distinct tissue distributions/properties: Creatine Kinase (CK) (CK-MM skeletal, CK-BB brain, CK-MB cardiac muscle — rises 4–6 h post-MI, peaks ~18–24 h, normalizes 48–72 h), LDH (5 isozymes LDH₁–LDH₅; flipped LDH₁ > LDH₂ in MI), and Troponins (cTnT / cTnI) (most sensitive & specific cardiac markers).
slides.remember: Competitive: ↑K_m, same V_max! Non-competitive: ↓V_max, same K_m! CK-MB = Cardiac isoenzymes in MI!
slides.q: Which kinetic pattern is characteristic of a reversible competitive enzyme inhibitor?
opts: Increased apparent K_m with unchanged V_max
slides.why: Competitive inhibitors compete at the active site, raising apparent K_m, while adding excess substrate can still achieve the same V_max.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Enzyme definition, activation energy & ES complex → Factors & K_m → Competitive vs non-competitive inhibition → Isoenzymes*** & MI markers (CK-MB, LDH, troponins) + diagnostic/therapeutic enzymes.

lessons.title: Biological Oxidation: ETC (Complexes I–IV & Inhibitors**), Oxidative Phosphorylation***, Uncouplers & Malate Shuttle*

slides.h: 1. Electron Transport Chain (ETC), ATP Synthesis Sites, Inhibitors** & Uncouplers
slides.p: The mitochondrial Electron Transport Chain (inner mitochondrial membrane) transfers electrons from NADH (Complex I) and FADH₂ (Complex II) via Coenzyme Q (ubiquinone) and Cytochrome c to O₂ (Complex IV → H₂O), pumping H⁺ into the intermembrane space to drive ATP synthase (Complex V / chemiosmotic hypothesis):
bullets: Sites of ATP Synthesis & ETC Inhibitors**: Proton pumping occurs at Complexes I, III, and IV (~2.5 ATP per NADH; ~1.5 ATP per FADH₂). Complex I inhibitors: Rotenone, barbiturates (amobarbital), piercidin A. Complex II inhibitors: Carboxin, malonate. Complex III inhibitors: Antimycin A, BAL. Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) inhibitors: Cyanide (CN⁻), carbon monoxide (CO), hydrogen sulfide (H₂S), azide. ATP synthase inhibitor: Oligomycin.

Uncouplers & Thermogenin: Uncouplers (2,4-dinitrophenol, thermogenin / UCP1 in brown adipose tissue) dissipate the H⁺ proton gradient as heat without ATP synthesis (electron transport & O₂ consumption continue/increase!).
slides.remember: ETC pumps H⁺ at Complexes I, III, IV! Cyanide/CO block Complex IV! Uncouplers (DNP, Thermogenin/UCP1) make HEAT instead of ATP!
slides.q: How do uncouplers of oxidative phosphorylation (such as 2,4-dinitrophenol or brown-fat thermogenin/UCP1) affect electron transport and ATP synthesis?
opts: They block both electron flow and oxygen consumption completely
They dissipate the proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane, generating heat rather than ATP while allowing electron transport to proceed
They convert ADP into AMP without oxygen
slides.why: Uncouplers allow protons to re-enter the matrix without passing through ATP synthase, uncoupling oxidation from phosphorylation and releasing energy as heat.

slides.h: 2. Substrate-Level Phosphorylation & Malate–Aspartate Shuttle*
slides.p: Contrast ATP generation mechanisms and cytosolic NADH transport into mitochondria:
bullets: Substrate-Level vs Oxidative Phosphorylation: Substrate-level phosphorylation forms ATP/GTP directly by transferring a phosphate group from a high-energy metabolic intermediate without O₂ or ETC (e.g., phosphoglycerate kinase & pyruvate kinase in glycolysis; succinyl-CoA synthetase in TCA cycle). Oxidative phosphorylation uses the ETC proton gradient and O₂.

Malate–Aspartate Shuttle*: Transfers reducing equivalents of cytosolic NADH into mitochondria (heart, liver, kidney): cytosolic oxaloacetate + NADH → malate (malate dehydrogenase) → enters matrix → re-oxidized to oxaloacetate + matrix NADH (yielding ~2.5 ATP) → transaminated to aspartate and exported back.
slides.remember: Substrate-level phosphorylation = Direct phosphate transfer without ETC! Malate-aspartate shuttle preserves NADH equivalents for heart & liver!
slides.q: Which of the following is an example of substrate-level phosphorylation rather than oxidative phosphorylation?
opts: ATP synthesis driven by Complex V (ATP synthase) using the H⁺ gradient
ATP formation catalyzed by phosphoglycerate kinase or pyruvate kinase during glycolysis
Electron transfer from NADH to Coenzyme Q
Thermogenin-mediated heat production in brown fat
slides.why: Substrate-level phosphorylation directly transfers a high-energy phosphoryl group from a substrate molecule to ADP/GDP without requiring the ETC.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: ETC complexes (I–IV), proton-pumping ATP sites & inhibitors** → Oxidative phosphorylation & uncouplers/thermogenin → Substrate-level vs oxidative phosphorylation → Malate-aspartate shuttle*.

lessons.title: Molecular Biology: DNA Replication, Transcription, Genetic Code***, Wobble, Protein Biosynthesis*, PCR & Lac Operon

slides.h: 1. DNA Replication, Transcription, PCR & Lac Operon
slides.p: Genetic information flows via semiconservative, bidirectional DNA replication (5' → 3') and transcription (RNA polymerase, 5' → 3'):
bullets: DNA Replication & Inhibitors: Helicase unwinds, primase makes RNA primer, DNA polymerase III synthesizes leading strand continuously and lagging strand as Okazaki fragments (joined by DNA ligase); topoisomerases/gyrases relieve supercoiling (inhibited by fluoroquinolones/ciprofloxacin; eukaryotic topoisomerase inhibited by etoposide/camptothecin).

Transcription, Post-Transcriptional Modification & PCR: Eukaryotic pre-mRNA undergoes 5' 7-methylguanosine capping, 3' poly(A) tailing, and intron splicing (spliceosome); bacterial RNA polymerase is inhibited by rifampicin (actinomycin D binds DNA). PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) amplifies DNA in vitro via thermal cycling: Denaturation (~94–95°C) → Annealing (~50–65°C primers) → Extension (~72°C by thermostable Taq DNA polymerase).

Lac Operon (Inducible Prokaryotic Operon): Structural genes (lacZ β-galactosidase, lacY permease, lacA transacetylase) are repressed by lac repressor bound to operator in absence of lactose; allolactose (inducer) inactivates repressor (and low glucose + high cAMP–CAP activates transcription).
slides.remember: DNA synthesis is always 5' → 3'! PCR = Denature, Anneal, Extend (Taq polymerase)! Lac operon inducer = Allolactose!
slides.q: Which thermostable DNA polymerase is classically used to extend DNA primers during the extension step of Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)?
slides.why: Taq DNA polymerase withstands repeated high-temperature denaturation cycles (~95°C) during PCR amplification.

slides.h: 2. Genetic Code***, Wobble Hypothesis, Mutations* & Protein Biosynthesis* (Translation)
slides.p: Master the genetic code, mutations, and ribosomal translation:
bullets: Genetic Code*** & Wobble Hypothesis: Triplet codons (64 total: 61 sense encoding 20 amino acids + 3 stop/nonsense codons: UAA, UAG, UGA; AUG = start/methionine). Code is degenerate/redundant, unambiguous, nearly universal, and non-overlapping. Crick's Wobble Hypothesis explains base-pairing flexibility at the 3rd codon / 5' anticodon position (allowing one tRNA to recognize multiple synonymous codons).

Mutations* & rDNA: Point mutations (silent, missense, nonsense) or frameshift mutations caused by UV/radiation, base analogs, alkylating/deaminating agents; recombinant DNA technology uses restriction endonucleases, vectors, and ligases for gene cloning/insulin/vaccines.

Protein Biosynthesis* (Translation — 5' → 3' mRNA, N → C polypeptide): Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases charge tRNAs (uses ATP); initiation (initiation factors, fMet-tRNA_i in prokaryotes / Met-tRNA_i in eukaryotes), elongation (peptidyl transferase / 23S or 28S ribozyme, EF-Tu/eEF1A, translocation EF-G/eEF2), and termination (release factors at UAA/UAG/UGA). Inhibitors include streptomycin/aminoglycosides, tetracyclines, chloramphenicol, erythromycin/macrolides, puromycin, and diphtheria toxin (eEF2).
slides.remember: Stop codons = UAA, UAG, UGA! Wobble = 3rd base of codon / 1st base of anticodon! Peptidyl transferase is a RIBOZYME!
slides.q: Which three mRNA codons serve as termination (stop) codons that signal the end of translation?
slides.why: UAA, UAG, and UGA are stop (nonsense) codons recognized by release factors rather than aminoacyl-tRNAs.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: DNA replication & inhibitors → Transcription, RNA processing & PCR → Lac operon → Genetic code***, wobble hypothesis & mutations* → Protein biosynthesis* (initiation, elongation, termination & antibiotics) + rDNA.

lessons.title: Proteins (Structure, Classification, Peptides* & tRNA***), Nucleotides*, Antioxidants, Nutrition & Plasma Proteins*

slides.h: 1. Protein Structure**, Classification, Peptides*, tRNA*** & Nucleotides*
slides.p: Review macromolecular structure and function across Proteins and Nucleotides:
bullets: Protein Structure** & Classification: Primary (amino acid sequence & peptide bonds), Secondary (local folding via H-bonds: α-helix, β-pleated sheet), Tertiary (3D folding of a single polypeptide stabilized by hydrophobic interactions, H-bonds, disulfide bridges, ionic bonds), and Quaternary (multisubunit assembly, e.g., Hb). Classified functionally (enzymes, transport, structural/collagen, contractile, hormonal, defense/Ig) and structurally (simple vs conjugated proteins with prosthetic groups: glycoproteins, lipoproteins, metalloproteins, hemoproteins).

Biologically Important Peptides* & tRNA***: Glutathione (γ-glutamyl-cysteinyl-glycine) (antioxidant/redox buffer, amino acid transport), insulin, oxytocin, vasopressin/ADH, bradykinin, angiotensin II. tRNA*** ('cloverleaf' secondary / L-shaped tertiary structure) has an acceptor arm (3'-CCA end), anticodon loop, D-arm, and TψC arm to deliver specific amino acids during translation. Nucleotides* serve as energy currencies (ATP/GTP), metabolic carriers (UDP-glucose, CDP-choline), second messengers (cAMP, cGMP), and coenzyme components (NAD⁺, FAD, CoA).

Free Radicals & Antioxidants: Reactive oxygen species (ROS: superoxide O₂•⁻, H₂O₂, hydroxyl •OH) cause lipid peroxidation/DNA damage; neutralized by antioxidant enzymes (superoxide dismutase [SOD], catalase, glutathione peroxidase) and antioxidant vitamins/nutrients (Vitamin E [α-tocopherol — main membrane lipid antioxidant], Vitamin C, β-carotene, selenium).
slides.remember: tRNA 3' end = -CCA! SOD + Catalase + Glutathione peroxidase & Vit E/C = Antioxidant defense! ATP/cAMP/NAD⁺ = Nucleotide functions!
slides.q: Which terminal nucleotide sequence is present at the 3' acceptor end of all mature tRNA molecules where the amino acid is attached?
slides.why: Every functional tRNA ends with the 3'-CCA sequence (added post-transcriptionally by nucleotidyltransferase), with the amino acid esterified to the terminal adenosine.

slides.h: 2. Nutrition (PEM***, Kwashiorkor*, Dietary Fiber, BMR) & Plasma Proteins* (Albumin & Ig)
slides.p: Complete the remaining Paper 1 short-note units:
bullets: Nutrition (PEM***, Kwashiorkor*, Dietary Fiber & BMR): BMR is basal energy expenditure at rest/post-absorptive/thermoneutral conditions (affected by BSA/age/sex/thyroid hormones). Dietary fiber (insoluble cellulose & soluble pectin/gums) increases stool bulk, speeds transit, lowers postprandial glucose/cholesterol, and supports gut microbiota. Protein-Energy Malnutrition (PEM***) spans Marasmus (calorie + protein deficiency; severe wasting, NO edema) and Kwashiorkor* (protein deficiency > calorie deficit; pitting edema due to hypoalbuminemia, fatty liver, flaky-paint dermatosis, depigmented hair; treated with gradual calorie/protein refeeding, electrolyte/infection control).

Plasma Proteins* — Albumin & Immunoglobulins*: Albumin maintains plasma oncotic pressure (~25–28 mmHg), binds/transports bilirubin, free fatty acids, calcium, and drugs, and acts as a negative acute-phase protein. Immunoglobulin G (IgG — Y-shaped H₂L₂ with Fab & Fc regions, heavy/light chains, disulfide bonds) mediates secondary immune response, opsonization, complement activation, and placental transfer.
slides.remember: Kwashiorkor* = Edema (low albumin!) + Fatty liver + Skin/hair changes; Marasmus = Severe wasting, NO edema! IgG crosses placenta!
slides.q: Which clinical feature is characteristic of Kwashiorkor compared with marasmus in protein-energy malnutrition?
opts: Pitting edema (due to hypoalbuminemia) and fatty liver
Absence of edema with extreme subcutaneous fat loss alone
slides.why: Kwashiorkor is marked by protein deficiency out of proportion to calories, leading to hypoalbuminemia-induced edema and hepatic steatosis (fatty liver).

lessons.exam: SN order: Protein structure**, classification & conjugated proteins → Peptides* (glutathione) & tRNA*** → Nucleotide functions* → Free radicals & antioxidants (SOD, catalase, Vit E/C) → Nutrition (BMR, fiber, PEM***/Kwashiorkor*) → Plasma proteins* (albumin & Ig structure/function).

lessons.title: Carbohydrate Metabolism: Erythrocyte Glycolysis & Rapoport–Leubering, TCA Cycle*, HMP Shunt* & Glycogen / GSD*

slides.h: 1. Erythrocyte Glycolysis, Rapoport–Leubering Cycle & TCA Cycle (Amphibolic*)
slides.p: Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and rely solely on anaerobic glycolysis, with a specialized shunt regulating oxygen unloading:
bullets: Erythrocyte Glycolysis & Rapoport–Leubering Shunt: 1,3-Bisphosphoglycerate is converted by bisphosphoglycerate mutase to 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) → phosphatase → 3-phosphoglycerate (bypasses phosphoglycerate kinase, costing 1 ATP per cycle). 2,3-BPG binds deoxyhemoglobin β-chains, lowering O₂ affinity (shifting O₂–Hb curve right) to enhance O₂ delivery to tissues.

TCA (Citric Acid / Krebs) Cycle — Amphibolic Nature*: Acetyl-CoA (2C) + Oxaloacetate (4C) → Citrate (6C, citrate synthase) → ... → α-Ketoglutarate (5C, isocitrate dehydrogenase) → Succinyl-CoA (4C, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase) → Succinate (4C, GTP/ATP via substrate-level phosphorylation) → Fumarate (succinate dehydrogenase / Complex II) → Malate → Oxaloacetate (3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP/ATP per turn). Amphibolic because it is both catabolic (oxidizing fuels) and anabolic (citrate → fatty acids/cholesterol; α-KG → glutamate/purines; succinyl-CoA → heme; oxaloacetate → gluconeogenesis/aspartate).
slides.remember: 2,3-BPG shifts O₂–Hb curve RIGHT (unloads O₂)! TCA cycle is AMPHIBOLIC (catabolic + anabolic precursors)!
slides.q: How does 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) in erythrocytes affect oxygen transport?
opts: It increases hemoglobin's oxygen affinity and shifts the curve left
It binds preferentially to deoxyhemoglobin and decreases O₂ affinity (shifts curve right), promoting O₂ unloading to tissues
It converts lactate into glucose inside RBCs
slides.why: 2,3-BPG stabilizes the T (deoxy) conformation of hemoglobin, shifting the O₂–Hb dissociation curve to the right and facilitating oxygen release to tissues.

slides.h: 2. HMP Shunt (Pentose Phosphate Pathway)*, Glycogen Metabolism & Glycogen Storage Diseases*
slides.p: Compare the HMP shunt and glycogen pathways/disorders:
bullets: HMP Shunt* (Cytosolic — Oxidative & Non-Oxidative Phases): Generates NADPH (for fatty acid/cholesterol synthesis, steroid hydroxylation, and maintaining reduced glutathione [GSH] via glutathione reductase to protect RBCs against oxidative hemolysis) and ribose-5-phosphate (for nucleotide/nucleic acid synthesis); NO ATP is generated directly. G6PD deficiency causes hemolytic anemia triggered by primaquine, fava beans, or infections.

Glycogen Metabolism & Glycogen Storage Diseases* (GSD): Glycogenesis (glycogen synthase; branching enzyme) and Glycogenolysis (glycogen phosphorylase — rate-limiting, activated by glucagon/epinephrine in liver and epinephrine/AMP in muscle; inhibited by insulin). Key GSDs: Type Ia / Von Gierke's disease (glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency → severe fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, hyperlipidemia); Type V / McArdle's disease (muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency → painful muscle cramps/myoglobinuria on exercise).
slides.remember: HMP shunt makes NADPH (antioxidant GSH & lipogenesis) + Ribose-5-P! Von Gierke (GSD Ia) = Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency → Severe fasting hypoglycemia!
slides.q: Deficiency of which enzyme causes Von Gierke disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type Ia), characterized by severe fasting hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly?
slides.why: Glucose-6-phosphatase is required in liver (and kidney) to release free glucose into blood from glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; its deficiency causes fasting hypoglycemia.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Erythrocyte glycolysis & 2,3-BPG shunt → TCA cycle & amphibolic role* → HMP shunt* (NADPH & ribose-5-P, G6PD deficiency) → Glycogenolysis, hormonal regulation & Glycogen Storage Diseases* (Von Gierke, McArdle).

lessons.title: Lipid Metabolism: Cholesterol Synthesis*** & Atherosclerosis, β-Oxidation**, Ketosis, Lipoproteins* & Fatty Liver*

slides.h: 1. Cholesterol Synthesis*** (HMG-CoA Reductase), Atherosclerosis, Lipoproteins* & Fatty Liver*
slides.p: Cholesterol (27C) is synthesized mainly in liver cytosol/ER from acetyl-CoA (via mevalonate → squalene → lanosterol → cholesterol); HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting enzyme (inhibited by statins and cholesterol feedback; induced by insulin/thyroid):
bullets: Cholesterol Functions & Atherosclerosis: Precursor of bile acids, steroid hormones, and vitamin D; maintains membrane fluidity. Elevated LDL ('bad cholesterol' — delivers cholesterol to peripheral tissues) deposits oxidized LDL in arterial intima → foam cells & fibrous plaques (atherosclerosis → CAD/stroke); HDL ('good cholesterol') mediates reverse cholesterol transport from peripheral tissues back to liver.

Ketosis & Fatty Liver* / Lipotropic Factors*: Prolonged fasting or uncontrolled diabetes increases fatty acid oxidation & acetyl-CoA → hepatic ketogenesis (acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate, acetone); excessive ketone bodies cause ketonemia, ketonuria, and metabolic ketoacidosis (ketosis). Fatty liver (triacylglycerol accumulation in hepatocytes) is prevented/reversed by lipotropic factors (choline, methionine, betaine, lecithin, ω-3 fatty acids, Vitamin E) needed for VLDL assembly/export.
slides.remember: HMG-CoA reductase = Rate-limiting enzyme in Cholesterol synthesis (inhibited by Statins)! LDL = Atherogenic; HDL = Reverse cholesterol transport! Choline = Lipotropic factor!
slides.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step of cholesterol biosynthesis and is inhibited by statin drugs?
slides.why: 3-Hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA (HMG-CoA) reductase converts HMG-CoA to mevalonate—the committed, rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis—and is the target of statins.

slides.h: 2. β-Oxidation of Palmitic Acid (16C) — Pathway, Regulation & Energetics**
slides.p: Fatty acids are activated to fatty acyl-CoA in cytosol, transported into mitochondria via the Carnitine shuttle (CPT-I rate-limiting; inhibited by malonyl-CoA), and degraded two carbons at a time via β-oxidation:
bullets: Four Recurring Steps per Cycle: (1) Oxidation by acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (produces 1 FADH₂), (2) Hydration (enoyl-CoA hydratase), (3) Oxidation by β-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (produces 1 NADH), (4) Thiolytic cleavage by thiolase (releases 1 Acetyl-CoA).

Energetics of Palmitate (16C): Undergoes 7 cycles → yields 8 Acetyl-CoA, 7 NADH, and 7 FADH₂ (minus 2 ATP equivalents for initial activation; net ATP yield is calculated using ~2.5 ATP/NADH, ~1.5 ATP/FADH₂, and ~10 ATP/Acetyl-CoA in modern biochemistry, or classical 129 ATP).
slides.remember: CPT-I (carnitine shuttle) is the rate-limiting step of β-oxidation and is inhibited by Malonyl-CoA! Palmitate (16C) = 7 cycles → 8 Acetyl-CoA!
slides.q: Which enzyme in the carnitine shuttle acts as the rate-limiting control point for fatty acid entry into mitochondria and is inhibited by malonyl-CoA?
slides.why: CPT-I on the outer mitochondrial membrane controls acyl-carnitine formation and is inhibited by malonyl-CoA (the first intermediate of fatty acid synthesis) to prevent simultaneous synthesis and oxidation.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Cholesterol synthesis*** (HMG-CoA reductase, functions, LDL vs HDL & atherosclerosis) → β-oxidation of palmitic acid (CPT-I, 4 steps, cycles & energetics**) → Ketosis → Lipoproteins* & Fatty liver* / lipotropic factors*.

lessons.title: Minerals (Ca²⁺, PO₄³⁻, Fe, Cu, Zn, I), Starvation*, Acid–Base & Buffers**, DM, LFT** & Clearance**

slides.h: 1. Mineral Metabolism (Ca²⁺, PO₄³⁻, Fe, Cu, Zn, I) & Starvation Metabolism*
slides.p: Master key minerals and metabolic adaptation to starvation:
bullets: Calcium*, Phosphorus*, Iron*, Copper, Zinc & Iodine: Ca²⁺ & PO₄³⁻ form hydroxyapatite in bone/teeth; Ca²⁺ also acts as an intracellular second messenger (via calmodulin/troponin C) and coagulation factor IV, regulated by PTH, calcitriol, and calcitonin (absorption aided by calcitriol/protein/acid; hindered by phytates/oxalates/high phosphate). Iron (absorbed in duodenum/upper jejunum as Fe²⁺ via DMT1; transported as transferrin; stored as ferritin/hemosiderin) is needed for Hb/myoglobin/cytochromes (deficiency → microcytic hypochromic anemia). Copper (ceruloplasmin, cytochrome oxidase, lysyl oxidase — Wilson's/Menkes), Zinc (carbonic anhydrase, alkaline phosphatase, insulin storage, zinc fingers), and Iodine (T₃/T₄ synthesis).

Starvation Metabolism* (Short-Term & Prolonged): Early fasting relies on liver glycogenolysis & gluconeogenesis (amino acids/lactate/glycerol); prolonged starvation shifts to lipolysis & ketogenesis to spare glucose for brain/RBCs and conserve muscle protein.
slides.remember: Iron = DMT1 (Fe²⁺) + Transferrin + Ferritin! Calcium = PTH/Calcitriol + Calmodulin second messenger! Starvation shifts to Ketones to spare protein!
slides.q: In which form and oxidation state is dietary non-heme iron primarily absorbed across the apical membrane of duodenal enterocytes via DMT1?
slides.why: Divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1) transports ferrous iron (Fe²⁺) across the apical enterocyte membrane.

slides.h: 2. Acid–Base Balance & Buffers**, Blood Glucose / DM, LFT** & Renal Clearance**
slides.p: Complete the major Paper 2 clinical & metabolic LAQ/SN topics:
bullets: Acid–Base Balance, Buffers** & Metabolic Acidosis*: Normal arterial blood pH is 7.35–7.45, maintained by blood buffers (principal extracellular buffer = HCO₃⁻ / H₂CO₃ bicarbonate buffer [Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = 6.1 + log([HCO₃⁻] / (0.03 × PaCO₂))]; also Hb, phosphate, plasma proteins), respiratory compensation (hyperventilation lowers PaCO₂ in metabolic acidosis), and renal compensation (H⁺ excretion, NH₄⁺ & HCO₃⁻ regeneration). Metabolic acidosis (primary ↓HCO₃⁻, ↓pH — e.g., DKA, lactic acidosis, renal failure) is compensated rapidly by hyperventilation (Kussmaul breathing) and slowly by kidneys.

Blood Glucose Homeostasis, DM & Glycosuria: Normal fasting glucose is ~70–100 mg/dL (regulated by insulin [lowering] vs glucagon, epinephrine, cortisol, GH [raising]). In Diabetes Mellitus, insulin deficiency/resistance causes hyperglycemia; once blood glucose exceeds renal threshold (~180 mg/dL), glycosuria occurs alongside lipolysis/ketosis and proteolysis.

Liver Function Tests (LFT**) & Clearance Tests**: LFTs evaluate synthetic (albumin, prothrombin time), metabolic/detoxifying, and excretory functions (serum bilirubin [direct/indirect], alkaline phosphatase [ALP — rises in biliary obstruction], bile salts, AST/ALT). Creatinine clearance** (~90–125 mL/min) estimates GFR without needing dietary protein restriction (unlike urea clearance, which underestimates GFR due to tubular reabsorption).
slides.remember: Bicarbonate buffer = Main ECF buffer (pH 7.35–7.45)! Creatinine clearance estimates GFR! ALP rises in Obstructive liver disease!
slides.q: Which buffer system is the principal extracellular buffer of human blood plasma and is regulated by both the lungs (PaCO₂) and kidneys (HCO₃⁻)?
slides.why: The HCO₃⁻ / H₂CO₃ system is the major extracellular buffer in blood plasma, with PaCO₂ controlled by ventilation and HCO₃⁻ regulated by the kidneys.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Minerals (Ca²⁺/second messenger, PO₄³⁻, Fe, Cu, Zn, I) → Starvation metabolism* → Acid-base balance, buffers** & metabolic acidosis* → Blood glucose homeostasis, DM & glycosuria → LFT** & Creatinine/Urea clearance**.

lessons.title: Carbohydrates (GAGs***, Hyaluronic Acid), Lipids (Phospholipids, EFA, Digestion), Hormones, Cancer (Tumor Markers***), Detoxification, LCD & Radioisotopes**
lessons.tag: SN · *** (GAGs, Hormones, Cancer, Detox, LCD & Radioisotopes)

slides.h: 1. GAGs*** & Hyaluronic Acid, Lipids (Phospholipids, EFA, Digestion) & Hormones (cAMP*, Steroid)
slides.p: Master these high-yield Paper 2 short-note topics:
bullets: GAGs*** & Hyaluronic Acid: Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs / mucopolysaccharides) are unbranched heteropolysaccharides of repeating disaccharide units (acidic sugar + amino sugar, mostly sulfated — chondroitin sulfate, keratan sulfate, dermatan sulfate, heparan sulfate/heparin). Hyaluronic acid is non-sulfated and lacks covalent protein core (glucuronic acid + N-acetylglucosamine), providing viscous lubrication in synovial fluid and vitreous humor; GAG deficiencies cause mucopolysaccharidoses (Hurler/Hunter).

Lipids (Phospholipids, EFA & Digestion): Phospholipids (glycerophospholipids like phosphatidylcholine/lecithin [lung surfactant], cephalin, phosphatidylinositol [IP₃/DAG second messenger], cardiolipin [inner mitochondrial membrane]; sphingomyelin) are amphipathic membrane builders. Essential Fatty Acids (EFAs) — linoleic (ω-6) and α-linolenic (ω-3) — cannot be synthesized by humans (lack Δ¹²/Δ¹⁵ desaturases) and form eicosanoids/membranes. Dietary lipids are emulsified by bile salts and digested mainly by pancreatic lipase + colipase.

Hormone Mechanisms (Group I vs Group II, cAMP* & Steroids*): Group I (lipophilic steroid/thyroid hormones) bind intracellular/nuclear receptors to alter gene transcription. Group II (hydrophilic peptide/catecholamine hormones) bind cell-surface receptors using second messengers like cAMP* (adenylyl cyclase → ↑cAMP → activates Protein Kinase A [PKA]; e.g., glucagon, epinephrine β, ACTH, TSH, PTH, ADH-V₂) or IP₃/DAG/Ca²⁺.
slides.remember: Hyaluronic acid = NON-sulfated GAG! EFAs = Linoleic & α-Linolenic acid! cAMP activates Protein Kinase A (PKA)!
slides.q: Which glycosaminoglycan (GAG) is uniquely non-sulfated and abundant in synovial fluid and vitreous humor?
slides.why: Hyaluronic acid is an unbranched, non-sulfated glycosaminoglycan that imparts high viscosity and resilience to synovial fluid and connective tissues.

slides.h: 2. Cancer (Tumor Markers***, Oncogenes**), Detoxification**, LCD (Electrophoresis*, Chromatography*, Flame Photometry) & Radioisotopes**
slides.p: Complete all remaining Paper 2 Biochemistry short notes:
bullets: Cancer — Tumor Markers***, Oncogenes** & Carcinogens*: Proto-oncogenes (normal growth-promoting genes) mutate into oncogenes** (e.g., Ras, Myc, ErbB2/HER2) driving uncontrolled proliferation alongside loss of tumor suppressors (p53, Rb) and chemical/radiation/viral carcinogens. Key tumor markers***: AFP (hepatocellular carcinoma, yolk sac tumor), CEA (colorectal/GI cancers), CA-125 (ovarian cancer), PSA (prostate cancer), hCG (choriocarcinoma/hydatidiform mole).

Detoxification** (Phase I & Phase II Conjugation**): Makes lipophilic xenobiotics/drugs/bilirubin more water-soluble for excretion: Phase I (oxidation via cytochrome P450 monooxygenases, reduction, hydrolysis) introduces/exposes functional groups; Phase II (conjugation**) attaches glucuronate (UDP-glucuronyl transferase), sulfate (PAPS), glycine, glutathione, acetate, or methyl groups.

LCD & Radioisotopes**: Electrophoresis* separates charged molecules (proteins/nucleic acids) in an electric field based on charge/size/pI; Chromatography* separates mixtures by differential partitioning between mobile and stationary phases (paper, TLC, column, affinity, HPLC); Flame photometer measures Na⁺, K⁺, Li⁺ by emission intensity when aspirated into a flame. Radioisotopes** (e.g., ¹³¹I for thyroid imaging/therapy, ³²P, ¹⁴C, ⁹⁹mTc) are used in metabolic tracing, RIA/imaging, and radiotherapy.
slides.remember: Tumor markers: AFP (liver), CEA (colon), CA-125 (ovary), PSA (prostate)! Phase II = Conjugation (glucuronide, sulfate, glycine, glutathione)! Electrophoresis = Electric field separation!
slides.q: Which phase of xenobiotic biotransformation (detoxification) involves conjugation with glucuronic acid, sulfate, glycine, or glutathione to increase water solubility?
slides.why: Phase II reactions conjugate xenobiotics or their Phase I metabolites with polar molecules such as UDP-glucuronate, PAPS (sulfate), glycine, or glutathione for excretion.

lessons.exam: SN order: GAGs*** & Hyaluronic acid → Phospholipids, EFA & lipid digestion → Group I/II hormones & cAMP* → Tumor markers***, oncogenes** & carcinogens* → Detoxification (Phase I & Phase II conjugation**) → Electrophoresis*, Chromatography*, Flame photometer & Radioisotopes**.
